newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S. delegation says Pyongyang refuses to change.
newsitem.headline: U.S. delegation says Pyongyang refuses to change.

text.p: North Korea told the largest-ever U.S. delegation to the communist state that Washington must lift economic sanctions against it and not try to change its centralised economic system, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.

The delegation, led by Porter Goss, chairman of the U.S. House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and including seven Congress members, flew into Seoul on Tuesday to brief South Korean officials on its three-day visit to North Korea, the officials said.
On Wednesday, the seven are due to meet South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha and U.S. General John Tilelli, commander of the 37,000 U.S. troops stationed in South Korea.
Seoul foreign ministry officials said the visit by the congressmen was the largest yet by U.S. officials.
"The North Koreans stressed the need for the lifting of U.S. sanctions and for additional food aid," a U.S. embassy official said of their visit.
"The North Koreans also made clear they will refuse to abandon their centralised political and economic systems," he added.
South Korean and U.S. officials have argued that the Stalinist state's highly centralised farm policies are partly responsible for its chronic food shortages.
Seoul said the North had an annual food shortage of between one and two million tonnes since the 1980s and that floods in 1995 and 1996 only worsened the situation.
The U.S. congressmen went to the reclusive North shortly after the two Koreas, the United States and China held their first four-nation meeting in New York last week.

Senior officials of the four nations failed to set an agenda for formal talks proposed by Seoul and Washington aimed at hammering out a permanent peace mechanism on the Korean peninsula, the last flashpoint of the Cold War, but agreed to meet again on September 15.
The Korean War ended in 1953 with an armistice agreement, but no permanent peace treaty has been signed.

Pyongyang's negotiators have repeatedly demanded more food assistance during the preparatory negotiations but Seoul and Washington ruled out any large-scale aid until the four nations begin substantive peace talks.

The United States and South Korea have led international efforts to provide food supplies to the Stalinist North, pledging $54 million and $16 million, respectively, so far this year through the United Nations World Food Programme.

The South Korean Red Cross, which promised a further $20 million worth of aid, said on Tuesday it would deliver 8,000 tonnes of corn and 1,400 tonnes of sorghum to the famine-stricken North between August 20-26.
North Korea-watchers in Seoul said North Korea's leadership sought better ties with the United States as a means to rescue its collapsing economy.
Shortly before flying to Seoul, Goss told a news conference in Tokyo that North Korea was unwilling to deal with South Korea until President Kim Young-sam ended his five-year term next February.
"They absolutely want nothing to do with the present leadership," Goss said.
The South Korean president has been a daily target of abuse from North Korean official media since he refused to mourn the death of North Korea's founding father, "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung, in 1994.
